description: The object is a Lego plate situated on the linear track feeder, positioned past the ramp. It remains stable and parallel to the track's movement direction, showing no signs of being pushed off or falling vertically like in rejection cases (pre-trap, post-track, or trap). The behavior matches the expected normal process where the part moves unhindered across the trap and continues forward.

The object remained on the linear feeder throughout the observed sequence without exhibiting signs of pre-trap rejection, post-track rejection, or falling off. The part successfully moved towards and past the ramp while staying within the track boundaries.

The input video sequence shows a lego roundplate on a linear vibration feeder. The part is positioned on the track, to the right of the ramp structure (part trap). It appears static or vibrating in place across the frames, consistent with the normal "linear vibration feeding simulation" described where objects seem still in space due to synchronous frequency. The plate is flat and fully supported by the feeder track, not falling or sliding off sideways (which would be a pre-trap or post-track rejection). Its position relative to the ramp indicates it has successfully navigated past the trap structure and landed on the exit section. As the description states, "As long as the roundplate is still on the track, then no anomalies has occured." Therefore, the behavior is normal.

The object moves from the left side of the track towards the ramp, climbs it unhindered, falls onto the feeder section on its right, and continues moving forward. This matches the normal process behavior described: 'move towards the ramp -> Climb the ramp unhindered -> Fall off the ledge onto the right side of the ramp linear feeder -> Move forwards on the linear feeder'. There are no visual indications of rejection or abnormal orientation.

The input video sequence shows a roundplate moving along a linear feeder track. It approaches the central ramp structure, climbs it without obstruction, and traverses across the top edge in a manner consistent with the normal process description. There is no visual evidence of part rejection (such as tumbling or falling off sideways) or deviation from the expected forward motion. The behavior matches the sub-sampled normal video process provided in the context.

The video sequence shows a lego roundplate on the linear track before reaching the trap ramp. The part is oriented correctly and appears to be moving forward along the feeder due to the vibration. There are no visual indications of the part being pushed off the track laterally (pre-trap or post-track rejection) nor falling off the edge. The behavior aligns with the normal process described where the object progresses from the left side towards the right.

Based on the analysis of the provided images, the roundplate lego part is observed moving across the linear feeder towards and over the ramp (trap). The sequence of images shows the object maintaining contact with the track throughout its movement. There are no visual indications in the provided frames that the part was pushed off the track vertically while traversing the ramp (post-trap rejection) or before entering it (pre-trap rejection). The behavior aligns with the normal process description where the object moves towards and across the trap.

The roundplate part is observed moving linearly from left to right across the feeder track. It successfully approaches, climbs, and passes over the central ramp (trap) structure without any indication of falling off, tilting, or rejection. Following the ramp, it continues moving forward on the linear feeder surface, adhering to the described normal process behavior.

The video sequence shows a lego roundplate on a linear vibration feeder that appears to be stuck or jammed in the part trap (ramp structure) for the entire duration. Unlike the normal process where the object should move forward along the track, climb the ramp unhindered, and then fall off onto the right-side feeder to continue moving, this sequence shows the roundplate remaining stationary on top of the ramp/trap structure without traversing or falling through it. The object is jammed/stuck before successfully completing the traversal/falling phase (which would be post-trap), indicating a failure at the trap location consistent with pre-trap rejection behavior (pushed onto/into trap but not passed through).

The roundplate part remains on the linear feeder surface throughout all frames of the sequence, moving along the track without exhibiting any signs of post-track rejection (falling off vertically after the ramp) or pre-trap rejection. It does not show evidence of being pushed from the track boundary while still oriented parallel to it, nor is there a vertical orientation indicating it is falling off due to rotation. Based on the rule that no anomalies occur as long as the roundplate remains on the track, this process behavior is normal.

The lego roundplate moves linearly from left to right, climbing the ramp (trap) and falling off the ledge onto the right side of the feeder as expected. There is no visual evidence of the part being pushed laterally or oriented in a way that deviates from the normal process description.

The image shows a roundplate lego part on a linear track that appears to be following the normal process. The part is positioned on the track and moving in the expected direction without any indication of being pushed off the track or encountering an obstruction like the ramp in an anomalous manner. There are no visual cues suggesting pre-trap or post-track rejection behavior.

The input video sequence images are visually consistent with the provided RAG retrieved normal data images. The position of the Lego roundplate part on the linear feeder and its relationship to the ramp do not exhibit any anomalies such as falling off the track, being pushed off the pre-trap or post-trap sections. The observed behavior matches the standard process pattern where the part moves along the track towards the ramp without rejection.

The video sequence appears consistent with the described normal process behavior for a linear vibration feeding simulation. The input images show the part (white roundplate) on the grey track, which is vibrating at a frequency where the object seems still in space, a characteristic explicitly mentioned in the normal data description. There is no visual evidence of push-off rejection (pixels outside track boundary) or an orientation suggesting falling off the track. The part is positioned on the ramp structure but appears to be within bounds and stable enough to not indicate specific anomalous failure modes like pre-trap or post-track rejection based on pixel overlap with the feeder boundaries.

The analysis of the input video sequence indicates an anomalous behavior. The first four images show the LEGO roundplate part approaching and climbing the ramp structure in a manner consistent with normal feeding. However, images 5 and 6 reveal a critical deviation: the part appears to be wedged or pushed vertically against the geometry of the ramp (specifically, under the overhang of the central trap structure). This interaction occurs prior to the part successfully crossing over the ramp onto the right side, which would be the expected "falling off" phase. The part is visually obstructed by the ramp's structure in a way not observed in the normal reference images or sub-sampled process videos, where parts sit flush on top. This corresponds to 'pre-trap rejection', as the part has been pushed into an anomalous position relative to the track and trap before it could fall off the ramp onto the linear feeder."

The video sequence displays a part (grey rounded plate) moving along the linear feeder. The object is seen traversing towards the ramp and maintaining its position on the track surface throughout all frames. There is no visual evidence of the part falling off, tilting unexpectedly, or being pushed into a rejection state before or after the ramp. The motion is consistent with normal feeding behavior.

The provided video sequence shows a linear feeder track with a trap/ramp section. No lego roundplate part is visible or moving in the frames. Since there is no part to demonstrate anomalous behavior such as pre-trap rejection, post-track rejection, or movement anomalies, and the scene matches the normal configuration of an empty or starting track, it is not classified as an anomaly.

The object (lego roundplate) moves towards the ramp and reaches the edge. Instead of falling over the ramp to move forward to the right as in normal process, it appears to be jammed or wedged vertically against the side wall/edge of the ramp structure. This deviation prevents the normal transition across the trap, fitting the anomaly category of being pushed vertical to movement direction prior to successfully falling/falling over the ramp.

The input video sequence consists of frames showing the linear feeder track but does not depict the expected Lego roundplate part engaging with or climbing the ramp (trap). The absence of the object performing the defined normal process—specifically, failing to climb over the trap as seen in the subsampled normal data—is consistent with a pre-trap rejection anomaly where the part was likely rejected from the track before reaching the ramp stage.

The input video sequence exhibits anomalous behavior where the object initially appears on the linear track but, in later frames (specifically images 9 and 10), is oriented vertically and is visually pushed off the linear feeder's boundary on the right side of the ramp. This contradicts the normal process of unhindered movement across the ramp, as the part ends up non-overlapping with the track surface rather than continuing to move forwards on it.
